## Yesterday in 30 seconds
`pwd` shows where you are, `ls PATH` looks somewhere without moving, and `cd PATH` moves you. Absolute paths start with `/` and work from anywhere; relative paths are read from where you stand. Shortcuts: `.` here, `..` up, `~` home, `cd -` back.

## Why this matters
When a tutorial says "edit the config", "check the logs" or "it's installed in /usr/bin", it assumes you know this map. Knowing where things live lets you find a config file, a log or a program without guessing, and in WSL it decides whether your project runs fast or slow.

## The concept
On Windows, each drive has its own tree (`C:\`, `D:\`). Linux has **one single tree** starting at `/`, and every folder has a fixed job. The layout is almost the same on every Linux system (it follows the *Filesystem Hierarchy Standard*), so once you learn it here, it works on any server you ever SSH into.

Think of it like a well-organised office building: every floor has a purpose, and you don't store the coffee machine in the server room.

| Folder | What lives there | Rough Windows equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | The root. The top of the whole tree. | `C:\` (but for everything) |
| `/home` | One folder per user. Yours is `/home/<you>`, also written `~`. Your projects go here. | `C:\Users` |
| `/root` | Home folder of the admin user *root*. Not the same as `/`. | The Administrator's profile |
| `/etc` | System-wide configuration: plain text settings files. | Registry + settings files |
| `/var` | *Variable* data that grows and changes: logs (`/var/log`), caches, databases. | `C:\ProgramData`, log folders |
| `/usr` | Installed programs and their files. Commands live in `/usr/bin`. | `C:\Program Files` |
| `/tmp` | Scratch space anyone can write to. Can be cleaned automatically. | `%TEMP%` |
| `/mnt` | Where other drives are attached (*mounted*). In WSL, `/mnt/c` is your Windows C: drive. | Drive letters |

A few others you'll see: `/bin` and `/sbin` are shortcuts to `/usr/bin` and `/usr/sbin` on modern Ubuntu, `/opt` holds some third-party software, and `/proc`, `/sys` and `/dev` are special "virtual" folders the kernel fills in (you don't store things there).

## Commands
Run on Ubuntu 24.04 as a normal user `dev`. Only `/mnt/c` couldn't be run on the test machine, because it isn't WSL.

### 1. See the whole top level: ls -F /
```bash
ls -F /
```
```output
bin@
bin.usr-is-merged/
boot/
dev/
etc/
home/
lib@
lib.usr-is-merged/
lib64@
lost+found/
media/
mnt/
opt/
proc/
root/
run/
sbin@
sbin.usr-is-merged/
srv/
sys/
tmp/
usr/
var/
```
- `/` is the path, so this lists the root without moving you. `-F` marks folders with `/`.
- Names ending in `@` (`bin@`, `lib@`) are **shortcuts** (symbolic links) to folders inside `/usr`. Links are Day 45.
- In WSL you'll likely also see `init` and `snap`. Don't worry about exact matches; look for the big ones in the table.

### 2. Homes: ls /home and ls /root
```bash
ls /home
```
```output
claude
dev
ubuntu
```
On your WSL you'll probably see just one folder: your username. Now try the admin's home:

```bash
ls /root
```
```output
ls: cannot open directory '/root': Permission denied
```
- That's normal. Only the admin can look inside `/root`. Normal users own their own folder in `/home` and nothing else. Permissions are Module 3.

### 3. Configuration lives in /etc: cat /etc/os-release
`cat` prints a file's contents to the screen (Day 10 covers it properly). This file says which Linux you're running:

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
```
```output
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS"
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="24.04"
VERSION="24.04.4 LTS (Noble Numbat)"
VERSION_CODENAME=noble
ID=ubuntu
ID_LIKE=debian
...
```
- Config in Linux is mostly **plain text files** like this, in `/etc`. Examples: `/etc/hostname` (the machine's name), `/etc/hosts` (Day 57), `/etc/nginx/` if you install nginx.
- You can *read* most of `/etc`, but changing it needs admin rights: `touch /etc/test` as a normal user gives `touch: cannot touch '/etc/test': Permission denied`.

### 4. Logs live in /var/log: ls /var/log
```bash
ls /var/log
```
```output
README
alternatives.log
apt
bootstrap.log
btmp
dpkg.log
faillog
fontconfig.log
journal
lastlog
postgresql
private
redis
wtmp
```
- `dpkg.log` and `apt/` record software installs. `postgresql` and `redis` appeared because those are installed on the test machine: installed services put their logs here. Yours will differ. Reading logs is Day 39.

### 5. Programs live in /usr/bin: ls -l /usr/bin/ls
Even `ls` itself is just a file:

```bash
ls -l /usr/bin/ls
```
```output
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 142312 Jan 23  2026 /usr/bin/ls
```
- `-l` gives the long format. The `x` letters mean it's executable (a program); `root root` means the admin owns it. You'll decode every column on Day 16.
- When you type `ls`, the shell finds this file in `/usr/bin` and runs it (how it knows where to look is Day 41 and Day 44).

### 6. Your Windows drive: /mnt/c (WSL only)
```bash
ls /mnt/c/Users
```
- In WSL this lists the folders in your Windows `C:\Users`, including your Windows username. So your Windows Desktop is at `/mnt/c/Users/<WindowsName>/Desktop`. Other drives follow the same pattern: `D:` is `/mnt/d`.
- Going the other way, from inside WSL you can run `explorer.exe .` to open the current Linux folder in Windows File Explorer. It shows up under a path like `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\<you>`.

## Try it now (in WSL)
1. Run `ls -F /` and match at least five names to the table above. Which entries end in `@`?
2. Run `cat /etc/os-release` and find your exact Ubuntu version. Then run `cat /etc/hostname` to see your machine's name.
3. Run `ls /var/log`, then `ls /usr/bin`. That second list is long: every command you'll learn lives there. Look for `ls`, `cd` (not there — it's built into bash), and `python3`.
4. Run `cd /mnt/c/Users` then `ls`. Find your Windows username, `cd` into it, and `ls Desktop`. Then `cd ~` to get back home.
5. From your home folder run `explorer.exe .` and look at the path in File Explorer's address bar. This is the safe way to see your Linux files from Windows.

## Common mistakes
- **Keeping your projects on /mnt/c.** It works, but every file access crosses from Linux to Windows, so `git status`, `npm install` and builds are much slower. Files there also all look like `rwxrwxrwx` in `ls -l`, and Windows editors may add CRLF line endings that break shell scripts. Keep code in `~/projects` and open it from Windows with `explorer.exe .` or VS Code's WSL extension.
- **Editing Linux files through Windows' hidden AppData folder.** WSL's disk lives in a file somewhere under `C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\...`. Don't go digging there; changing Linux files that way can corrupt them. Use `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\...` (what `explorer.exe .` opens) instead.
- **Mixing up `/`, `/root` and `~`.** `/` is the top of everything, `/root` is the admin's home, and `~` is *your* home (`/home/<you>`). "Permission denied" in `/root` or when writing to `/etc` doesn't mean something is broken; you just aren't the admin. `sudo` is Day 15.
- **Saving important work in `/tmp`.** It's scratch space and may be emptied automatically. Anything you want to keep goes in `~`.

## Cheat sheet
| Path / command | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `/` | Root: the top of the single tree |
| `/home/<you>` = `~` | Your files and projects |
| `/root` | Admin's home (not `/`) |
| `/etc` | System config (text files) |
| `/var/log` | Log files |
| `/usr/bin` | Installed commands and programs |
| `/tmp` | Temporary scratch files |
| `/mnt/c` | Windows C: drive (WSL) |
| `ls -F /` | See the top level, folders marked / |
| `cat /etc/os-release` | Which Linux version you're on |
| `explorer.exe .` | Open the current folder in Windows Explorer (WSL) |

## Why this matters
When a tutorial says "edit the config", "check the logs" or "it's installed in /usr/bin", it assumes you know this map. Knowing where things live lets you find a config file, a log or a program without guessing, on your own machine or on any server you SSH into.

## The concept
Linux has **one single tree** starting at `/`, and every folder has a fixed job. Extra disks and USB sticks don't get their own letter; they are attached (*mounted*) as a folder somewhere in the tree. The layout follows the *Filesystem Hierarchy Standard*, so it's almost the same on Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch and nearly every server.

Think of it like a well-organised office building: every floor has a purpose, and you don't store the coffee machine in the server room.

| Folder | What lives there |
|---|---|
| `/` | The root. The top of the whole tree. |
| `/home` | One folder per user. Yours is `/home/<you>`, also written `~`. Your projects go here. |
| `/root` | Home folder of the admin user *root*. Not the same as `/`. |
| `/etc` | System-wide configuration: plain text settings files. |
| `/var` | *Variable* data that grows and changes: logs (`/var/log`), caches, databases. |
| `/usr` | Installed programs and their files. Commands live in `/usr/bin`. |
| `/tmp` | Scratch space anyone can write to. Often emptied on reboot. |
| `/media` | Where removable drives appear automatically on desktop distros, usually `/media/<you>/<drive>` or `/run/media/<you>/<drive>`. |
| `/mnt` | An empty spot for mounting drives by hand, usually by an admin. |
| `/dev` | Devices as files: disks show up as `/dev/sda`, `/dev/nvme0n1`, etc. |

A few others you'll see: `/bin` and `/sbin` are shortcuts to `/usr/bin` and `/usr/sbin` on modern Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian and Arch; `/opt` holds some third-party software; `/boot` holds the kernel and boot files; and `/proc` and `/sys` are special "virtual" folders the kernel fills in (you don't store things there).

## Commands
Run on Ubuntu 24.04 as a normal user `dev`. Other distros give very similar output.

### 1. See the whole top level: ls -F /
```bash
ls -F /
```
```output
bin@
bin.usr-is-merged/
boot/
dev/
etc/
home/
lib@
lib.usr-is-merged/
lib64@
lost+found/
media/
mnt/
opt/
proc/
root/
run/
sbin@
sbin.usr-is-merged/
srv/
sys/
tmp/
usr/
var/
```
- `/` is the path, so this lists the root without moving you. `-F` marks folders with `/`.
- Names ending in `@` (`bin@`, `lib@`) are **shortcuts** (symbolic links) to folders inside `/usr`. Links are Day 45.
- The `*.usr-is-merged` folders are an Ubuntu detail; Fedora and Arch don't have them. Don't worry about exact matches; look for the big ones in the table.

### 2. Homes: ls /home and ls /root
```bash
ls /home
```
```output
claude
dev
ubuntu
```
On your machine you'll probably see just one folder: your username. Now try the admin's home:

```bash
ls /root
```
```output
ls: cannot open directory '/root': Permission denied
```
- That's normal. Only the admin can look inside `/root`. Normal users own their own folder in `/home` and nothing else. Permissions are Module 3.

### 3. Configuration lives in /etc: cat /etc/os-release
`cat` prints a file's contents to the screen (Day 10 covers it properly). This file says which Linux you're running:

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
```
```output
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS"
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="24.04"
VERSION="24.04.4 LTS (Noble Numbat)"
VERSION_CODENAME=noble
ID=ubuntu
ID_LIKE=debian
...
```
- Config in Linux is mostly **plain text files** like this, in `/etc`. Examples: `/etc/hostname` (the machine's name), `/etc/hosts` (Day 57), `/etc/nginx/` if you install nginx.
- You can *read* most of `/etc`, but changing it needs admin rights: `touch /etc/test` as a normal user gives `touch: cannot touch '/etc/test': Permission denied`.

### 4. Logs live in /var/log: ls /var/log
```bash
ls /var/log
```
```output
README
alternatives.log
apt
bootstrap.log
btmp
dpkg.log
faillog
fontconfig.log
journal
lastlog
postgresql
private
redis
wtmp
```
- `dpkg.log` and `apt/` record software installs on Debian/Ubuntu. On Fedora you'd see `dnf`-style logs; on Arch, `pacman.log`.
- `postgresql` and `redis` appeared because those are installed on the test machine: installed services put their logs here.
- `journal/` holds the system journal. Fedora and Arch keep most system logs there instead of in text files, so their `/var/log` looks emptier. Reading logs (including `journalctl`) is Day 39.

### 5. Programs live in /usr/bin: ls -l /usr/bin/ls
Even `ls` itself is just a file:

```bash
ls -l /usr/bin/ls
```
```output
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 142312 Jan 23  2026 /usr/bin/ls
```
- `-l` gives the long format. The `x` letters mean it's executable (a program); `root root` means the admin owns it. You'll decode every column on Day 16.
- When you type `ls`, the shell finds this file in `/usr/bin` and runs it (how it knows where to look is Day 41 and Day 44).

### 6. Where drives appear: lsblk and /media
`lsblk` (**l**i**s**t **bl**oc**k** devices) shows your disks and where each one is attached in the tree:

```bash
lsblk
```
```output
NAME  MAJ:MIN RM  SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
vda   254:0    0  256G  0 disk /
vdb   254:16   0  9.6M  1 disk /opt/rclone
...
```
- The test machine is a virtual machine, so its disks are called `vda`, `vdb`. On a laptop you'll see `nvme0n1` or `sda`, split into partitions like `nvme0n1p2`.
- **MOUNTPOINTS** is the key column: it shows which folder each disk appears as. The one mounted at `/` is your main system disk.
- Plug in a USB stick on a desktop distro and it appears under `/media/<you>/` (Ubuntu, Mint) or `/run/media/<you>/` (Fedora, Arch).

## Try it now
1. Run `ls -F /` and match at least five names to the table above. Which entries end in `@`?
2. Run `cat /etc/os-release` and find your exact distro and version. Then run `cat /etc/hostname` to see your machine's name.
3. Run `ls /var/log`, then `ls /usr/bin`. That second list is long: every command you'll learn lives there. Look for `ls`, `cd` (not there — it's built into bash), and `python3`.
4. Run `lsblk` and find the disk mounted at `/`. If you're on a desktop, plug in a USB stick, run `lsblk` again and spot the new line and its mount point.
5. Run `xdg-open .` from your home folder. It opens the current folder in your desktop's file manager (it won't work on a server with no desktop).

## Common mistakes
- **Mixing up `/`, `/root` and `~`.** `/` is the top of everything, `/root` is the admin's home, and `~` is *your* home (`/home/<you>`). "Permission denied" in `/root` or when writing to `/etc` doesn't mean something is broken; you just aren't the admin. `sudo` is Day 15.
- **Saving important work in `/tmp`.** It's scratch space and is often emptied on reboot. Anything you want to keep goes in `~`.
- **Looking for a USB drive in the wrong place.** It's not `/dev/sdb` (that's the raw device, not its files). Its files are where it's *mounted*: check the MOUNTPOINTS column of `lsblk`, usually under `/media` or `/run/media`.

## Cheat sheet
| Path / command | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `/` | Root: the top of the single tree |
| `/home/<you>` = `~` | Your files and projects |
| `/root` | Admin's home (not `/`) |
| `/etc` | System config (text files) |
| `/var/log` | Log files |
| `/usr/bin` | Installed commands and programs |
| `/tmp` | Temporary scratch files |
| `/media` · `/run/media` · `/mnt` | Where drives are attached |
| `ls -F /` | See the top level, folders marked / |
| `cat /etc/os-release` | Which Linux version you're on |
| `lsblk` | Disks and where they're mounted |
| `xdg-open .` | Open the current folder in the file manager |

quiz.explain: `/var` holds changing data; logs are in `/var/log`.
`/` is the top; `/root` is root's home. Normal users can't open it.

quiz.explain: `ls -F /` lists the root and marks directories with `/` and links with `@`.

Why keep code under `~` instead of `/mnt/c`?
options: Linux tools are much slower there and permissions/line endings behave oddly
